source.title: How Much of a Probe Direction Lives in the Input Embedding? An Audit of Four Published Claims
source.citation: How Much of a Probe Direction Lives i…

record.tranche_reason: Applies the published difference-of-means refusal direction and full-stream directional ablation procedure to new chat-model checkpoints, then measures refusal-related outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study tests the refusal-direction claim (V1) with held-out predictive correlations and directional ablation. Its truth, sentiment, sycophancy, and conjunction-fallacy results do not test the listed refusal-claim versions. The paper cites claims about separate harmfulness and refusal directions but does not test that separation. It does not add the direction, perform weight edits, test jailbreaks or adversarial training, or transfer a fitted direction between models.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Arditi difference-in-means refusal direction (AdvBench harmful minus Alpaca harmless) and applies full-stream directional ablation to seven chat models, reporting held-out refusal log-odds changes with bootstrap CIs. That bears directly on V1's ablation claim. The paper's headline result is a predictive-correlation audit (embedding-partialled r, random-direction null). The authors say this does not test causal mediation: 'a FAIL does not falsify a causal claim.' Those rows are relinked to none and recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that predictive and causal evidence dissociate on two AdvBench cells (Llama-3-8B, Phi-3-mini): partial r falls to the random-direction null, yet ablation still suppresses refusals. Ablation effects, not probe correlation, should carry causal claims, and the two should be cited separately. The dissociation is dataset- and checkpoint-conditioned and does not invalidate single-direction claims. The authors also note large harmless-prompt ablation effects, suggesting the mean-difference axis absorbs covariate features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the published difference-of-means refusal-direction fitting and full-stream directional-ablation procedure, with a held-out refusal-log-odds evaluation and additional embedding-partial and random-direction controls. It does not test addition or general capability preservation.
record.method_sensitivity: The refusal partial-correlation result changes with prompt set for Llama-3-8B: AdvBench FAIL versus Anthropic-CAA PASS. Results also depend on metric for Gemma-2-9B: a harmful-prompt log-odds null versus a rule-based refusal result described as PASS. Refusal-audit outcomes differ across checkpoints and held-out model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Embedding-partialled predictive audit. On AdvBench, 63% (Llama-3-8B) and 66% (Phi-3-mini) of the refusal direction's held-out correlation with refusal log-odds is inherited from the input-embedding projection, within or near a random-direction null. Five other models pass or are borderline, as do all four held-out families. Llama-3-8B passes when the direction is refit on Anthropic-CAA prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The difference-in-means refusal direction's predictive correlation with refusal reflects structure the network builds through depth, beyond the input-embedding projection.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a single GemmaScope SAE feature (771) on Gemma-2-9B gives Δharmful −0.84 with a 38% predictive drop. This is an SAE feature, not a difference-in-means direction. No row records it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single SAE features aligned with harmful-vs-harmless contrasts causally shape refusal.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code is planned for release upon publication
record.peer_reviewed: not stated; the text identifies the document as an anonymous ACL submission
record.problems: The main panel is a convenience sample from five model families. The refusal test fold has 50 harmful and 50 harmless prompts; the Llama-3-8B drop interval [29%, 123%] is broad. The authors note heuristic verdict thresholds, unstratified bootstrap intervals, finite random-null sampling, and possible prompt-template/surface-feature explanations. General capability preservation is not measured, and the study does not report refusal rates demonstrating complete removal.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant refusal results were omitted. Other audited behaviors (truth, sentiment, sycophancy, and conjunction fallacy) do not bear on the listed refusal-claim versions.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; preservation of general capabilities; complete removal of refusal measured as a refusal or compliance rate (only log-odds shifts are given).
No weight edit or abliterated released models.
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training.
No multi-direction or cone comparison. The paper only cites Wollschläger et al. when interpreting covariate features.
Zhao et al. (2025) is cited as consistent with the findings, but harm vs refusal is not tested.
No transfer of a fitted direction across languages or models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the predictive partial-correlation rows to V1. These were relinked to none because they measure probe correlation, not ablation or addition effects, and the authors explicitly separate them from causal claims. Ablation rows stay partial because no baseline refusal rate or post-ablation refusal rate is reported, so removal cannot be confirmed. Rows R15–R17 mix ablation deltas with predictive drop percentages, and the unit of the rule-based Δ is not stated. The study is an anonymous ACL submission and is not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests; does not establish that ablation removes refusal completely or preserves general capabilities. The intervention results are refusal-related log-odds shifts and a rule-based refusal metric.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration test.
No test of jailbreak suppression of the direction or training against its ablation.
No experiment comparing a single direction with an affine set, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal.
Does not independently measure or intervene on harmfulness judgment separately from refusal; the discussion cites related work.
Directions are fitted separately for models and prompt sets; no same-direction transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models is tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or training stages.

relation.reason: Reports its own held-out ablation effects with bootstrap CIs on seven chat models, which bears on V1's ablation claim.

tranche.reason: Same method as Arditi: AdvBench minus Alpaca difference-in-means direction, projected out at every block. Measures are a teacher-forced refusal log-odds plus a rule-based variant using Arditi's refusal prefixes.

source_check.notes: The pack gives no [lN] ids, so l1–l4 follow the pack's order. The rule-based results (R15–R17) are in §4.4 'Two-metric robustness', not §4.5. Their unit is unstated. The paper gives no baseline log-odds or refusal rates, so no row shows how complete removal is. The Figure 2 caption says ablation suppresses refusal 'on every refusal cell', despite Gemma's log-odds null. The study is an anonymous ACL submission, and code is promised upon publication.

statements.problem: This study's Llama-3-8B result appears under a 'challenges' entry about ablation being 'weak or absent'. Here the effect is significant (CI excludes zero) and the authors say the ablation effect reproduces. The study's own verdict for this cell is limits_scope, not challenges.
